A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VRoPE research. All pages, equations, tables, and figures are readable. v3 ends with references; v4 includes Appendices A-E. The complete supplied material supports comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original video-understanding evaluations, retrieval experiments, attention visualizations, and ablations in Section 5 and Tables 1-4.

after.justification: v4 retains the original experiments and adds boundary-attention measurements, EventBench evaluations, robustness analyses, and larger-model results.

M1.justification: Most of Section 4 reformulates the existing four-direction encoding and H+W-1 frame stride. However, v3 Equation 8 assigns (u+, u-, v+, v-) to successive channel residues, whereas substituting v4 Equations 6-9 yields (u+, v+, u-, v-). Two directions therefore exchange frequency-channel assignments in the printed procedure, a limited methodological revision.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds EventBench's event-sequence evaluation and a separate training regime using OpenVid-1M and LLaVA-NeXT-790K, substantially extending the documented evaluation and training coverage. The original benchmarks remain. Section 5.1 also drops OneVision from the stated Qwen2 fine-tuning mixture, although the unchanged main results do not establish retraining.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain RoPE and RoPE-3D, with RoPE-2D, RoPE-Share, and RoPE-Compact retained in the variant ablation. Added experiments use the existing RoPE/RoPE-3D comparator set. The new Qwen2.5-VL citation does not introduce an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: v4 adds 8-frame Video-MME testing and a separate Qwen3-8B/SigLIP-2 configuration using 32 frames, 384-by-384 inputs, and approximately 1 million pre-training and 3 million instruction-tuning samples. Table 1 introduces boundary-attention measurements using instruction queries and video/text keys. The original 16-frame, 224-by-224 main evaluation setting is retained.

E4.justification: v4 adds boundary-attention diagnostics addressing cross-modal discontinuity (Table 1), Video-MME duration breakdowns (Table 7), sparse-frame robustness testing (Table 8), and a query-specific attention/error case study (Figure 5 and Appendix C). The original variant and component ablations remain, with the continuity component renamed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. Both use point estimates and qualitative significance language; the additional results retain that reporting practice.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in v3 Tables 1-4 are retained in v4 Tables 2-5. Added results cover boundary attention, EventBench, video durations, sparse sampling, and Qwen3-8B. For example, Table 8 reports VRoPE/RoPE accuracy of 40.9/38.9 with eight frames; Table 9 reports averages of 62.40/61.92 in the new 8B configuration, with mixed per-benchmark outcomes. These are newly reported results under their respective settings.

T1.justification: The formal VRoPE definition changes its coordinate-to-channel association, affecting which coordinate receives each channel-dependent RoPE frequency. The explicit t(H+W-1) temporal formula otherwise restates v3's recursive frame offset. Appendix A largely relocates the dimensional-adaptability argument, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: VRoPE preserves spatiotemporal structure, mitigates positional bias, and smooths video-text transitions to improve understanding and retrieval. Component renaming and broader experimental support do not materially redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands the mechanism explanation through vertex symmetry, frame-center alignment, and temporal-axis progression. Sections 3.4 and 5.3 interpret boundary attention and retained RoPE-3D retrieval weaknesses as evidence of discontinuity-related problems. Appendices B-C add robustness, generalization, and localization-error interpretations. Limitations now include 8B evaluations while retaining the unvalidated extensions to other modalities.

D1.justification: The abstract changes code availability from a future promise to a reported release, and Appendix E adds research-only model licensing information. Appendix B.4 documents the expanded model/data configuration, while Appendix D supplies explicit RoPE-Share and RoPE-Compact indexing rules. Section 4 also clarifies the initial position relative to preceding text. These materially expand reproducibility documentation.

R1.justification: v4 adds references for Qwen2.5-VL, EventBench, OpenVid-1M, SigLIP-2, and Qwen3, while removing the Vicuna, Qwen2, and Su multimodal-position reflection references. The central positioning against the limitations of RoPE-2D/RoPE-3D remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: Section 4 is substantially rewritten and reordered: symmetry precedes the renamed Temporal Centered Arrangement, replacing the rotation-led exposition. The introduction's component descriptions are revised accordingly, and dimensional adaptability moves from Section 4.3 to Appendix A. New appendices and acknowledgments extend the document structure, although much background and the conclusion remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, and v3's architecture Figure 2 and method Figure 4 are combined into an expanded v4 Figure 3. v4 adds boundary-attention Table 1, Appendix Tables 6-9, and case-study Figure 5. Existing attention and retrieval heatmaps are retained under renumbering. The component-ablation table moves, and RoPE-2D's continuity indicator is corrected to match the existing prose.

improvement.justification: v4 improves assessability through clearer method illustrations, boundary-attention measurements, duration and sparse-frame analyses, and validation with SigLIP-2/Qwen3-8B. It also reports code availability and adds implementation details. These provide useful additional support, but uncertainty estimates remain absent, and strong causal and superiority interpretations are insufficiently qualified by the observational attention evidence and mixed new benchmark results. The net quality improvement is limited.
